text: I'm Ajaykumar Balakannan. Most people just call me Ajay. I'm a data engineer based in Dallas. I finished my Master's in Data Science at the University of Maryland in May 2026, graduating with a 3.74/4.0. What I do is build the pipelines other people's work sits on top of, batch and streaming, on AWS and Databricks. Right now I'm at The Cigna Group running a HIPAA-compliant ELT pipeline over about 15TB of healthcare claims a day, plus a Kafka and Spark Structured Streaming service that answers member eligibility checks in under two seconds. Before that, a serverless ingestion layer at Maryland, a summer of job-market data science at Canaria, and a Databricks lakehouse at Siemens over industrial IoT data. Python and SQL are the daily drivers, PySpark and Airflow are the workhorses. I'm looking for full-time data engineering and data platform roles.

source: portfolio (self-description, grounded in the work below)
text: How I work. I own the whole path rather than handing off a stage of it. At Cigna that means the ingestion, the transformations, the quality gates and the alerting are all mine, because a pipeline that only half belongs to someone is the one that breaks quietly at 3am. I'm suspicious of data by default. That's why I put 240+ Great Expectations and AWS Deequ validation rules across Redshift and S3 at Cigna, and completeness checks at Maryland that caught schema drift before anything downstream noticed. I'd rather a job fail loudly than pass something wrong through. The numbers I care about are runtime, cost and reliability. Some specific ones, each from a different job so they don't get mixed up: at Cigna, 42% off end-to-end runtime from dynamic partition pruning and better join strategies, and 38% off compute by moving Pandas UDFs to native Spark SQL window functions. At Siemens, 25% less resource consumption and about $3,000 a month off cloud spend from query and partitioning work. At Maryland, 60% fewer manual interventions and failed retries across 50+ daily Airflow DAGs. I like problems where the constraint is real, like a fixed nightly window or a compliance boundary, because that's when the engineering actually has to be good rather than just clever.

My timeline, so the dates line up. Aug 2020 to May 2024: B.Tech in Electrical and Electronics Engineering at Sri Krishna College of Engineering and Technology, Coimbatore, India. Jan 2023 to Jul 2024: Data Engineer at Siemens in India, which overlapped my final year of the B.Tech and ran a couple of months past graduation. Sep 2024 to May 2025: Graduate Data Engineer at the University of Maryland in College Park, alongside my Master's. May 2025 to Aug 2025, so the summer of 2025: Data Science Intern at Canaria Inc. in New York. Sep 2025 to now: Data Engineer at The Cigna Group in Texas, which is my current role. May 2026: I graduated from Maryland with my Master's in Data Science. I'm living in Dallas and looking for full-time data engineering roles.

I did my Master's in Data Science at the University of Maryland, College Park, and graduated in May 2026 with a GPA of 3.74/4.0 (an older internal document says 3.78 from an earlier term). The coursework that mattered most was Natural Language Processing, Machine Learning, Big Data Systems, and Deep Learning. Maryland is a big public R1 school just outside Washington DC. A few of my NLP and deep learning course projects came out of that program, including the RNN comparison, the n-gram modeling work, and the gun violence coverage analysis.

text: My undergrad is a B.Tech in Electrical and Electronics Engineering from Sri Krishna College of Engineering and Technology (SKCET) in Coimbatore, India, Aug 2020 to May 2024, CGPA 8.4/10.0. SKCET is an autonomous private engineering college founded in 1998 and affiliated with Anna University, with NBA accredited programs and a spot in the NIRF engineering top 100. Coursework included Microcontrollers, Power System Analysis, Python, and Machine Learning in Energy Systems. I think coming from electrical engineering rather than CS is part of why I like systems that touch the physical world. The farmland detection project was hardware and vision together, not just a model in a notebook.

Since Sep 2025 I've been a Data Engineer at The Cigna Group, based in Texas. It's my current role. I orchestrated a HIPAA-compliant ELT pipeline on AWS Glue and PySpark that processes about 15TB of healthcare claims data daily, and cut end-to-end runtime by 42% using dynamic partition pruning and better join strategies. I built a real-time member eligibility validation system on Apache Kafka and Spark Structured Streaming that holds sub-two-second latency across 8,500+ concurrent API requests and improved data freshness by 87%. I deployed an automated data quality framework with Great Expectations and AWS Deequ, monitoring 240+ validation rules across Redshift and S3, which cut anomaly resolution time by 65% and lifted SLA adherence to 99.97%. I refactored the PySpark transformation jobs from Pandas UDFs to native Spark SQL window functions, dropping compute cost 38% and scaling to 4.2 billion records per batch cycle. And I implemented a Delta Lake layer on Databricks with ACID transactions and time travel, so a failed run rolls back to a point in time instead of being reprocessed from scratch, which cut reprocessing effort by 73%. Working on claims means HIPAA is a design constraint rather than a checklist at the end.

From Sep 2024 to May 2025 I was a Graduate Data Engineer at the University of Maryland in College Park, working there alongside my Master's. I created a serverless data ingestion pipeline on AWS using S3, Glue and Redshift, which cut data loading latency by 40% across 500+ research datasets. I engineered PySpark ETL jobs to cleanse and transform 2TB of raw institutional data, improving downstream analytics accuracy by 25% through stricter validation rules. I untangled the workflow dependencies with Apache Airflow, which reduced manual intervention and failed task retries by 60% across 50+ daily DAGs. I tuned Redshift distribution and sort keys and took 35% off query time for the financial reporting dashboards. And I set up proactive completeness checks with Great Expectations that sustained 99.5% completeness across the research datasets and surfaced schema drift before it caused downstream failures. It was a good place to learn orchestration properly, because research data arrives in whatever shape the researcher had on the day.

I was a Data Science Intern at Canaria Inc. in New York from May 2025 to Aug 2025, so the summer of 2025. I developed Python and SQL/PySpark pipelines over 15M+ job market records across ClickHouse and PostgreSQL, which surfaced trends and data quality issues that fed real production decisions. I designed and tuned a Gradient Boosting salary prediction model across 40,000+ US zip codes, engineering SOC code, seniority and company-level features into an auto-updating ClickHouse pipeline for real-time forecasting. I containerized and orchestrated the pipelines and ML workflows with Docker, Kubernetes and AWS (EC2 and S3), which improved scalability and resource utilization across their production systems. And I integrated LLM APIs, ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, along with text embeddings on the compensation datasets, iterating on prompt patterns until an insight-to-content workflow that used to be manual ran on its own. It's the one role on my CV that sits on the science side rather than the engineering side, and it's where a lot of my comfort with messy data at scale came from.

A bit about Canaria Inc., where I interned in summer 2025. Canaria is a New York based job market data startup, founded in 2022. They sell research grade labor market intelligence: roughly a billion deduplicated job postings enriched with 100+ fields, SOC occupation codes, salary signals, and a taxonomy of 40,000+ skills, plus company profiles and AI extracted compensation data. Their customers are in HR, recruitment, workforce analytics, and financial modeling. That context explains the shape of my work there. When your product is the dataset itself, a bad posting or a mis-scored salary is a defect that ships straight to clients. So most of my summer was anomaly detection, validation, and recalibration rather than modeling for its own sake.

A bit about The Cigna Group, where I work now. It's a US health services company headquartered in Bloomfield, Connecticut, and one of the largest healthcare companies in the country by revenue. It operates through two main businesses: Evernorth Health Services, which covers pharmacy benefits, specialty pharmacy and care services, and Cigna Healthcare, which is the insurance and benefits side. That shape explains my work. When the core of the business is adjudicating and paying claims for millions of members, the data is enormous, continuous, and legally sensitive, so the engineering problems are throughput, freshness and provability rather than novelty. Every pipeline I touch there is HIPAA-bound, which affects how data is stored, who can see it, and what has to be auditable afterwards.

A bit about Siemens, where I worked from Jan 2023 to Jul 2024. Siemens is a German industrial technology group headquartered in Munich, and one of the largest industrial manufacturers in Europe. TravelGenie is my AI travel planning system, built Dec 2025. It's at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/TravelGenie. It plans a trip by pulling flights, hotels, events, weather, currency, and traffic through one request instead of ten browser tabs. The architecture is seven standalone MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, Flight, Hotel, Event, Geocoder, Weather, Finance, and Traffic and Crowd, each doing exactly one job, with Claude orchestrating and chaining their outputs. So it geocodes a location, then searches flights and hotels near it, then checks the weather for those dates. Flight, hotel, and event data comes from SerpAPI. Open-Meteo and OpenStreetMap need no API key. It ships as a Streamlit web UI and a Slack bot, and the MCP servers can run directly inside Claude Desktop too. It deploys via Docker or AWS using ECS Fargate, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager, and CloudWatch, provisioned with CloudFormation. The part I'd point at is the benchmarking. I load tested EC2 against ECS Fargate under sustained and stress load at 50 to 100 concurrent users, and Fargate matched EC2's 460 requests per second on roughly half the compute. MIT licensed.

text: Farmland wildlife intrusion detection, Mar 2023, at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/Framland_Protection. It's a non-lethal alternative to electric fencing and chemical repellents for keeping wildlife off farmland. A camera watches the field continuously. YOLOv3 does real-time animal detection at around 90% accuracy, with non-maximum suppression to drop redundant boxes. Then a second validation stage, a CNN for species verification plus a Random Forest to filter false positives, cuts false alarms by about 40%. A confirmed detection triggers an Arduino controller that fires a deterrent matched to the animal: sound for nocturnal animals, light for herbivores like deer, water sprinklers for medium sized ones. Every detection gets logged with image, species, time, and location, which is useful for conservation and census work. One honest correction. The README's future work section mentions upgrading to YOLOv5, and YOLOv3 is what I actually implemented and demoed, even though a couple of later materials (a portfolio tag, one resume version) say YOLOv5. It won 2nd place out of 500+ teams and a $300 prize at the National Technocraft Hackathon (Technocraft Booth Project Competition 2022-23, held at COEP in Pune on 2nd May 2023), and the work was published in BIOGECKO, Vol 12 Issue 03, 2023. We built and tested a hardware prototype alongside the software.

Bitcoin price forecasting, 2025, a Qlik Sense project under causify-ai/tutorials (TutorTask146). End to end it does live BTC price collection, ARIMA and XGBoost forecasting at around 85% predictive accuracy, automated ingestion, validation and transformation workflows, and interactive Qlik Sense dashboards for real-time visibility into volatility and market drivers. It cut manual reporting effort by about 40%.

source: RealEstateModelling GitHub README + portfolio + public information about the company
text: The Sage Ventures multifamily real estate analytics pipeline, 2025, at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/RealEstateModelling. Being straight about this one: it's a self-built portfolio project, not client work. I simulated the data infrastructure, reporting, and BI of a multifamily real estate portfolio to show SQL, Python, Power BI, and Excel skills for a junior data analyst type role, and the underlying data is synthetic, generated with Faker. Sage Ventures is a real firm though, a Baltimore and Pikesville, Maryland real estate company founded in 2004 that acquires, develops, rehabilitates, and manages multifamily properties around the DC and Baltimore region. That's what I modeled the scenario on. The pipeline runs in one command (run_pipeline.py) across five phases. generate_data.py builds a SQLite DB and raw CSVs, feature_engineering.py creates 15+ engineered features, adhoc_analysis.py produces 5 business reports, excel_report.py builds a 7 sheet workbook, and visualize.py generates 10 charts. The data model goes properties to units to tenants to rent_roll, plus properties to maintenance and properties to occupancy_monthly. Stack is Python, SQLite, SQL, Pandas, openpyxl, Matplotlib, and Power BI. Some illustrative findings from the simulated portfolio: 67% average occupancy against a 93% target, $2.14M annual loss to lease, $19,864 in delinquency exposure, and 533 open maintenance tickets past SLA.

The CANARIA Anomaly Detection System at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/Version-1-anomaly is the job market anomaly detection work tied to my Canaria internship. It finds unusual patterns in job posting data at three levels: US level (geo_level by source), state level (state by source), and SOC occupation level (SOC code by source). Parquet files get read in configurable batches, 50,000 rows by default, cleaned and validated, then stored in MongoDB under a rolling window (45 days by default) so the models keep adapting to recent data without storage growing forever. Feature engineering generates 18 features per record: rolling statistics over 7, 14, and 28 days, temporal features like day of week and month, statistical measures like z-scores and MAD, and expanding window long-term patterns. The model layer is a 7 model ensemble, PyCaret's Isolation Forest, KNN, and SVM plus PyOD's HBOS, COPOD, OCSVM, and CBLOF. Scores get averaged for robustness and compared against per-segment quantile thresholds, with cooldown logic so it doesn't spam alerts. Output is CSV results with scores, plus logging and performance monitoring.

Resume Optimiser and Outreach Automation at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/Resume_Optimiser is two tools in one repo, built in 2026. First, a resume optimizer CLI (resume_api.py). You paste in a job description and get back a tailored one page LaTeX resume, a cover letter paragraph, and an email draft, generated through the Claude API and compiled with pdflatex. Second, an outreach web app in Next.js. You upload a contacts CSV, attach a resume, write one email template, preview every personalized message, and send the batch through Gmail via OAuth. It integrates with Apollo.io to find and reveal contacts at a target company across leadership and role matched tiers, and writes a custom paragraph per contact using Claude Haiku plus a free web search cascade (Tavily, Exa, Brave) to get real context on each person. There are guardrails that reject generic AI sounding phrasing or a too casual tone and retry with a correction. Cost and usage get tracked per call, tokens, cache hits, and USD, and surfaced in an analytics view, because I wanted to actually know what the thing costs to run.

BudgetPlay at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/BudgetPlay is a participatory budgeting simulator I built for an Anthropic Hackathon, Track 3, Governance and Accessibility. You explore how a city sized budget is allocated, move sliders to rebalance spending across categories, read a Claude generated plain language narrative explaining the tradeoffs of your reallocation, and optionally submit your budget as a vote grouped by region. A companion Government Pulse dashboard aggregates submissions so community averages can be compared against the official budget, with percentage point shifts by category and short recommendation blurbs. Stack is Node.js and Express on the backend, a static frontend with Tailwind, Chart.js, and vanilla JS, and the Anthropic Messages API for the narrative endpoint. The budget data is sample and educational, not a real government budget.

A comparative analysis of RNN architectures for sentiment classification, from my UMD coursework, at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/Sentiment-Analysis. I implemented and compared plain RNN, LSTM, and Bidirectional LSTM on the IMDb movie review dataset, varying activation functions (sigmoid, ReLU, tanh), optimizers (Adam, SGD, RMSprop), sequence lengths of 25, 50, and 100 words, and gradient clipping on and off, to see how each choice moves classification performance.

N-gram language modeling and evaluation, UMD coursework, at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/N_Gram_Modelling. I implemented and evaluated Maximum Likelihood Estimation n-gram language models from unigram through 4-gram on the Penn Treebank dataset, looking at the tradeoff between n-gram order and the role of smoothing and backoff in handling data sparsity, with perplexity evaluation and text generation.

A comparative analysis of gun violence coverage across news outlets, from my UMD NLP coursework, at github.com/AjaykumarBalakannan/Comparative_Analysis_HW5. I used NLP techniques including coreference resolution with spaCy to analyze how CNN, Fox News, The New York Times, and The Wall Street Journal portray victims and shooters across gun violence incidents, over a dataset of 100 articles, 25 per outlet.

My team took 2nd place out of 500+ teams and a $300 prize at the National Technocraft Hackathon (Technocraft Booth Project Competition 2022-23, hosted by the Alumni Association of the College of Engineering Pune and the COEP Charitable Foundation USA, held 2nd May 2023) for the farmland wildlife intrusion detection project. It was a team project during my B.Tech at Sri Krishna College. The findings were later published in BIOGECKO, Vol 12 Issue 03, 2023, a New Zealand biology journal, on YOLO based AI detection with automated deterrents.
